source_refs.note: 1.1.4 field properties (i)-(v), Note on order axioms, Example 2 (book p. 3); PDF 8-8.

blocks.text: 1.1.4 Properties of the Fundamental Operations on Complex Numbers
It can easily be verified that the set \(C\) satisfies all the field axioms, i.e. it possesses the properties of real numbers. To explain some of the points, we observe the following:

items: Every complex number \((a, b)\) has the additive inverse \((-a, -b)\), i.e. \[(a, b) + (-a, -b) = (0, 0)\]
The multiplicative identity is \((1, 0)\), i.e. \[(a, b)(1, 0)\] \[= (a\cdot1 - b\cdot0,\ b\cdot1 + a\cdot0)\] \[= (a, b)\] \[= (1, 0)(a, b)\]

Every non-zero complex number (i.e. a number not equal to \((0, 0)\)) has a multiplicative inverse. The multiplicative inverse of \((a, b)\) is \[\left(\dfrac{a}{a^2+b^2},\ \dfrac{-b}{a^2+b^2}\right)\] because \[(a, b)\left(\dfrac{a}{a^2+b^2},\ \dfrac{-b}{a^2+b^2}\right)\] \[= (1, 0),\] the identity element, and this also equals \[\left(\dfrac{a}{a^2+b^2},\ \dfrac{-b}{a^2+b^2}\right)(a, b)\]

blocks.title: Note
blocks.text: The set \(C\) of complex numbers does not satisfy the order axioms. In fact, there is no sense in saying that one complex number is greater or less than the other.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
"Field axioms" means the familiar rules of real-number arithmetic: addition and multiplication are closed, commutative and associative; there are identities \((0,0)\) and \((1,0)\); every number has an additive inverse and every non-zero number a multiplicative inverse; and multiplication distributes over addition (point (v)). So you may calculate with complex numbers just as with real numbers.
Why can't complex numbers be ordered? Suppose \(i > 0\). Multiplying both sides by the positive number \(i\) gives \(i \cdot i > 0\), i.e. \(-1 > 0\), which is false. Suppose instead \(i < 0\); then \(-i > 0\) and \((-i)(-i) > 0\), i.e. \(-1 > 0\), again false. Since \(i \ne 0\), no ordering obeying the order axioms is possible. (Our explanation, not printed in the book.)

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Where does the inverse come from? Write \((a, b)\) as \(a + ib\) and multiply top and bottom by the conjugate:
\[\dfrac{1}{a + ib} = \dfrac{a - ib}{(a + ib)(a - ib)}\]
\[= \dfrac{a - ib}{a^2 + b^2}\]
which is the pair \(\left(\frac{a}{a^2+b^2}, \frac{-b}{a^2+b^2}\right)\). We need \((a, b) \ne (0, 0)\) so that \(a^2 + b^2 \ne 0\).
Illustration (ours): the inverse of \((3, 4)\) is \(\left(\frac{3}{25}, \frac{-4}{25}\right)\), because \(3^2 + 4^2 = 25\).

blocks.title: Example 2
steps:
Given: \(z_1 = (4, 2)\), \(z_2 = (3, -1)\).
To find: \(\frac{z_1}{z_2}\).
Method: write the pairs in the form \(a + ib\), then multiply the numerator and the denominator by the conjugate of the denominator so that the denominator becomes real.

Step 1: write in the form \(a + ib\)
\[\dfrac{z_1}{z_2} = \dfrac{(4, 2)}{(3, -1)}\]
\[= \dfrac{4 + 2i}{3 - i}\]
Why: the pair \((a, b)\) means \(a + ib\).

Step 2: multiply top and bottom by the conjugate \(3 + i\)
\[\dfrac{4 + 2i}{3 - i} \times \dfrac{3 + i}{3 + i}\]
Why: \(\frac{3+i}{3+i} = 1\), so the value does not change; and \((3-i)(3+i)\) has no \(i\) left, so the denominator becomes real.

Step 3: the numerator
\[(4)(3) + (4)(i) + (2i)(3) + (2i)(i)\]
\[= 12 + 4i + 6i + 2i^2\]
\[= 12 + 10i - 2\]
\[= 10 + 10i\]
Why: each term multiplies each term; then \(i^2 = -1\) turns \(2i^2\) into \(-2\).

Step 5: divide
\[\dfrac{z_1}{z_2} = \dfrac{10 + 10i}{10}\]
\[= 1 + i\]
Why: both the real part and the imaginary part are divided by 10.

Check:
\[(1 + i)(3 - i) = 3 - i + 3i - i^2\]
\[= 3 + 1 + 2i\]
\[= 4 + 2i\]
This is \(z_1 = (4, 2)\), so the answer is right.

blocks.title: Exam tip
blocks.text: To divide complex numbers, always multiply the numerator and the denominator by the conjugate of the denominator. The denominator becomes \(c^2 + d^2\), a real number, and the answer can be written as \(x + iy\).

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. \(C\) satisfies all the field axioms.
2. Additive identity \((0, 0)\); additive inverse of \((a, b)\) is \((-a, -b)\).
3. Multiplicative identity \((1, 0)\); inverse of \((a, b) \ne (0,0)\) is \(\left(\frac{a}{a^2+b^2}, \frac{-b}{a^2+b^2}\right)\).
4. \(C\) is not ordered: \(z_1 > z_2\) has no meaning for complex numbers.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.text:
Writing the inverse of \(a + ib\) as \(\frac{1}{a} + \frac{1}{ib}\). Wrong: use the conjugate.
Forgetting the minus sign in the inverse: the second component is \(\frac{-b}{a^2+b^2}\).
Writing \((3-i)(3+i) = 9 - 1 = 8\). Since \(i^2 = -1\), it is \(9 - (-1) = 10\).
Comparing complex numbers, e.g. "\(3 + 2i > 1 + i\)". Only their moduli (1.1.5), which are real, can be compared.
